steps: Hold your dominant hand up near the side of your head.
Wave it gently from side to side with your palm facing outward.
Keep eye contact and smile while you wave.
tip: The same wave is also used for 'hi' and 'bye' in BSL.

steps: Raise your dominant hand near the side of your head, palm facing outward.
Wave it gently from side to side.
Hold eye contact briefly, then turn away naturally.
tip: 'Bye' uses the same wave; keep the movement relaxed, not exaggerated.

steps: Touch the fingertips of your flat dominant hand to your chin.
Move your hand down and away from your face in one smooth motion.
Mouth the words 'thank you' silently as you sign.
tip: A small, quick movement is all you need in everyday conversation.

steps: Touch the fingertips of your flat dominant hand to your chin.
Move your hand slightly forward and away from your face.
Mouth the word 'please' silently as you sign, since this is what distinguishes it from 'thank you'.
tip: 'Please' and 'thank you' share the same manual sign in BSL; the mouth pattern carries the meaning.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist.
Hold the fist against the centre of your chest.
Move it in small circles against your chest.
tip: Mouth 'sorry' silently while signing to make it unmistakable.

steps: Close your hand into a fist.
Nod the fist up and down, like a head nodding.
Repeat the nodding motion a couple of times.
tip: Pair the fist nod with an affirmative facial expression.

steps: Extend your index and middle fingers.
Tap them against your thumb, like a mouth opening and closing as it says 'no'.
Add a slight head shake for emphasis if you like.
tip: The tapping fingers look like lips mouthing the word 'no' — that visual link makes it easy to remember.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up.
Rest your dominant closed hand, thumb up, on top of that flat palm.
Keep the position steady, or lift it slightly.
tip: The thumbs-up resting on the open palm reads visually as 'lifting someone up'.

steps: Raise your dominant hand, palm facing outward, fingers together.
Push it firmly forward toward the person or thing you want to stop.
Keep your expression serious to match a 'halt' command.
tip: BSL has no single all-purpose 'stop': this is the halt command. For 'stop an activity', BSL signs more like CEASE/FINISH.

steps: Bend the index finger of your dominant hand into a hook.
Start with the hand in front of your body.
Pull the bent finger toward yourself, like beckoning.
tip: Repeat the pull for emphasis, e.g. calling someone from a distance.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, then twist your wrist so the palm turns outward.
tip: Add a slight forward lean and a wanting expression on your face to sell the meaning.

steps: BSL uses the same sign for NEED as for WANT.
Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, finishing with a small outward twist of the wrist.
tip: Since NEED shares its sign with WANT, sign extra context around it so your meaning is clear.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat with fingers together, thumb folded across (a closed flat hand).
Tap your chest with it once or twice.
tip: Mouth the English word 'like' silently as you tap — mouthing is normal and expected in BSL.

steps: Make a fist with your thumb sticking out.
Tap the side of your head with your thumb, repeating the tap.
tip: Make the thumb tap land visibly on the head — a vague wave near the face will not read clearly.

steps: Make the KNOW sign: fist with thumb out, tapping the side of your head.
While signing, shake your head side to side with a slight frown.
In BSL the headshake itself carries the negation — it happens during the sign, not after it.
tip: Practise the headshake as part of the sign from day one; BSL negation is simultaneous, not sequential.

steps: Form the BSL letter M with your dominant hand.
Tap it against your open non-dominant palm twice.
tip: Practise the two-handed BSL M shape on its own first, so the double tap lands cleanly on the palm.

steps: Hold out your non-dominant hand with just the index and middle fingers extended.
Tap those two fingers twice with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand — this is the BSL letter F signed twice.
tip: Keep the two taps on the same fingertips and crisp; sloppy contact can look like a different sign.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your body, one resting over the other, arms bent as if cradling something.
Rock your hands gently from side to side, like holding a baby.
tip: Slow the rocking right down when learning — the cradling mime reads best at half speed.

steps: Clasp your non-dominant hand with your dominant hand in front of your body.
Make a small up-and-down bobbing movement with the clasped hands.
tip: Keep the bob small and gentle — a big shake looks like washing your hands.

steps: Extend only the index finger of your dominant hand.
Brush it along your chin, moving from your dominant side toward the other side.
tip: Use the chin, not the cheek — BOY and GIRL live on different parts of the face.

steps: Make a closed fist with your index finger pointing up.
Brush the finger down your cheek twice.
tip: Practise BOY then GIRL back to back — cheek versus chin — to lock in the difference.

steps: Bring your fingertips and thumb together into a bunched shape.
Tap the bunched fingers against your mouth twice.
tip: Make the double tap rhythmic, like taking two bites — the timing makes it instantly readable.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a loose C shape, as if holding a cup.
Lift the hand up to your mouth.
Tip your wrist toward your face, as though taking a drink from the cup.
tip: Keep the motion small and repeat it once or twice; mouthing the word 'drink' helps hearing learners remember it.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat, fingers together and palm facing down.
Place the hand at the front of your throat.
Make two short downward movements against the throat.
tip: The contact is light — a gentle tap against the throat, not a squeeze.

steps: Place your dominant hand flat on your stomach.
Rub the stomach in a small circular motion a few times.
Add a hungry facial expression to reinforce the meaning.
tip: A small circle is enough — big sweeping movements look exaggerated rather than natural.

steps: Bring your dominant hand, held flat, up to your throat.
Sweep the hand downward across the throat.
Repeat the downward movement once more for emphasis.
tip: Keep the fingers together and the sweep short; the throat location is what carries the meaning.

steps: Hold both hands in a closed flat shape, fingertips touching thumbs.
Place your dominant hand just in front of the other at chest height.
Tap the dominant hand against the non-dominant hand repeatedly.
tip: Two or three taps in a steady rhythm reads most naturally; mouthing 'more' helps beginners.

steps: Open both hands, palms facing each other.
Tap the palm of your dominant hand against the palm of your non-dominant hand.
Repeat the tap twice with a bright, happy facial expression.
tip: The facial expression does half the work — smile while you sign it, or it reads flat.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat and vertical in front of your face, thumb tucked in.
Drag the hand downward from nose level to chin level.
Wear a sad expression while you sign.
tip: Let your face droop slightly — in BSL the expression carries the emotion, not just the hands.

steps: Curl both hands into claw shapes, fingertips bent.
Place the claws on your chest.
Drag both hands upward and outward, away from your body, with an angry face.
tip: Keep the movement firm and decisive — a weak, slow movement reads as frustration rather than anger.

steps: Place both hands in closed flat shapes on your chest, thumbs touching the chest.
Twist both hands downward until the palms rest flat against your chest.
Let your shoulders and head droop slightly with a weary expression.
tip: Exaggerate the droop of the shoulders — the sinking body language is what makes 'tired' readable.

steps: Extend the little finger of each hand, keeping the other fingers closed.
Rest the edges of both little fingers on your chest.
Brush both little fingers downward along your body, then repeat the movement once.
tip: Think of the little fingers as sickness draining downward out of the body — that image fixes the movement in memory.

steps: Hold both hands open in front of your body, palms facing toward you.
Move the hands alternately up and down.
Add a grimace that matches the severity of the pain.
tip: Bigger alternating movements and a stronger grimace read as worse pain — scale the expression to the meaning.

steps: Curl both hands into claw shapes.
Tap both claws against your chest repeatedly.
Widen your eyes with a frightened expression.
tip: Tap quickly for a startled 'scared'; tap more slowly for a lingering sense of fear.

steps: Flatten both hands, palms facing inward.
Cross both hands over your chest on the left side.
Give a small warm press inward with a gentle smile.
tip: Think of pressing something precious to your heart — that is the image the sign is built on.

steps: Bend the fingers of your dominant hand so the fingertips point downward.
Tap your fingertips against the far side of your chest.
Then tap them against the near side of your chest.
tip: Tap lightly with the fingertips, not the whole hand, and keep your elbow relaxed.

steps: Hold both hands open in front of your body with palms facing inward.
Move both hands downward together until they finish flat and horizontal.
tip: The same sign also covers 'dark' — lower the hands smoothly, as if night is falling.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of you, palms facing up, fingers together and flat.
Bounce both hands up and down together in unison, repeating the motion.
tip: Keep both hands moving together at the same speed — the repetition marks 'right now'.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm in front of you with the wrist facing up.
Tap the top of that wrist twice with your dominant index finger.
tip: Tap where a watch would sit — the sign points at the wrist as if checking the time.

steps: Hold your dominant index finger up in front of your body.
Wiggle your hand in short side-to-side movements.
Keep a questioning expression on your face while you sign.
tip: The facial expression is part of the sign — raise your eyebrows to mark it as a question.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm out in front of you.
With your dominant thumb, draw a small cross on top of your opposite forearm.
tip: Only one written BSL source was found for this sign, and hospital signs vary regionally — confirm the local variant with a Deaf signer.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out flat, palm facing up.
Tap the inside edge of that palm twice with your dominant index finger.
tip: BSL uses the TOILET sign for 'bathroom' — the dictionary has no separate bathroom sign.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of you with fingers closed, as if gripping a steering wheel.
Move both hands up and down in opposite directions, like turning the wheel.
tip: Keep the movements small and alternating — it mimes turning a steering wheel.

steps: Hold both flat hands up at an angle in front of you, fingertips pointing up.
Bring the fingertips together so your hands form the shape of a roof.
tip: The same sign also covers 'home'.

steps: Hold your dominant hand up with index and middle fingers extended together.
Bend your wrist side to side while moving your hand downward.
tip: Keep the two fingers pressed together as your hand travels down.

steps: Point to yourself over your heart to sign 'I'.
Flatten both hands and cross them gently over your chest, as if pressing something into your heart, to sign 'love'.
Point at the other person to sign 'you'.
tip: Sign the three parts as one smooth, flowing sequence with a warm expression.

steps: Hold your dominant index finger up and wiggle it side to side with a questioning look, to sign 'what'.
Point your index finger at the person you are asking, to sign 'your'.
Touch your forehead with your index and middle fingers held together, then twist your wrist so the fingertips point forward, to sign 'name'.
tip: In BSL the topic comes first, so fluent signers often order the signs 'name' then 'what'.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist, knuckles facing forward.
Raise the closed fist to the side of your chin, knuckles pointing outward.
Tap the knuckles against your chin twice, with two crisp beats.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your cheek throughout both taps.
Nod once as you finish, so it reads as a definite number.
tip: The same sign covers maths and mathematics — context tells them apart.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands, fingers pressed firmly together.
Press the palms together in front of your chest, fingertips pointing forward.
Swing both hands outward and apart twice, like opening a book's covers.
Keep your palms facing each other as the hands open and close.
Mouth the word 'book' silently while you sign, to fix the meaning.
tip: Think of two covers swinging open — the double motion names the object itself.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like a page.
Form a V with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand.
Sweep the V fingertips down across the palm, zigzagging from wrist toward fingers.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingertips glide over the page.
Fix your gaze on the moving fingertips, as if your eyes are reading along.
tip: The V's fingertips are 'eyes' scanning the lines — mime them reading each word.

steps: Open your dominant hand beside your head, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Hold the open hand just to the side of your temple, palm angled inward.
Draw the hand slightly backward while your fingers close together into a pinch.
Keep the motion small and close to the head, finishing with pinched fingertips.
Keep a thoughtful, attentive expression, as if an idea has just landed.
tip: One-handed at the temple is the most widely taught form; some regions use both hands moving toward the forehead instead.

steps: Curve both hands into full C shapes, thumbs opposing the fingertips.
Hold the two C hands in front of your chest, a few inches apart.
Tip the hands toward each other in alternating inward pouring motions.
Keep the pouring smooth and rhythmic, like decanting between two beakers.
Wear a curious, inquisitive expression — science is about wondering.
tip: Picture pouring liquid back and forth between two cupped beakers.

steps: Press both flat hands together in front of your chest, palms touching.
Open and close the hands repeatedly, like flicking through a book's pages.
Travel both hands sideways as they open and close, covering a short distance.
Keep your palms facing each other through every opening motion.
Glance along the path of the moving hands, as if scanning a shelf.
tip: The book sign repeated while moving sideways — a whole shelf of books.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, index finger and thumb slightly apart.
Hold the C hand upright in front of your torso, fingers pointing forward.
Move the hand straight down once, in one clean stroke.
Keep the C handshape steady and the palm facing sideways through the drop.
Mouth the word 'student' silently, since the same sign also means person and pupil.
tip: One manual sign covers student, person and pupil — mouthing picks the English word.

steps: Close both hands into relaxed fists in front of your body.
Bring the fists together so the outer edges meet at chest height.
Tap the hands against each other twice, with two light, even beats.
Keep both palms facing inward and the wrists relaxed through the taps.
Keep the taps small and crisp — big swings start to look like clapping.
tip: Two light taps of fist on fist — the rhythm of stacking sheets of paper.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and index finger into a small circle.
Spread your remaining fingers open behind the pinched thumb-and-index circle.
Hold the hand in front of your chest and draw a question mark in the air.
Trace the hook first, then dot it with a short downward flick.
Raise your eyebrows and lean slightly forward, the classic questioning face.
tip: You are literally drawing a '?' in the air — hook, then dot.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like paper.
Pinch your dominant index fingertip against your thumb, as if holding a pen.
Make small side-to-side scribbling motions across the open palm surface.
Keep your dominant palm angled sideways and the strokes quick and light.
Keep the writing hand moving — a still pen on a palm reads as pointing.
tip: The same writing motion covers pen, pencil and scribble — the tool is in the handshape.

steps: Extend the index fingers of both hands, tucking the other fingers away.
Raise both hands to the sides of your head, fingers pointing upward.
Hold the hands briefly at temple height, framing your head.
Keep both palms facing each other across the sides of your head.
Mouth the word 'teacher' silently, since regional variants of this sign exist.
tip: Two index fingers raised like antennae at the head — mouthing fixes it as teacher.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a C shape, thumb opposing the fingertips.
Hold the C hand in front of your chest, fingers pointing forward.
Rotate your wrist downward, sweeping the hand over as if marking each person.
Repeat the downward rotation two or three times, shifting slightly sideways.
Keep your expression open and inclusive — you are gathering a crowd.
tip: Several regional variants exist; this wrist-rotating version is among the most widely used.

steps: Pinch both thumbs against index fingers to form two F handshapes.
Hold both F hands in front of your body, a few inches apart.
Move the hands together in a small horizontal clockwise circle.
Keep the F circles intact and the motion smooth through the loop.
Soften your face with a warm expression — family is an affectionate sign.
tip: Two F hands circling like a family gathered around a table; some regions use an open hand instead.

steps: Open your dominant hand with the fingers together, thumb relaxed.
Place the open hand around your chin, fingertips near the jawline.
Slide the hand downward while fingers and thumb close together, tracing a beard.
Keep the palm angled toward your face through the downward slide.
Finish with the hand just below the chin, fingers lightly pinched.
tip: Traces a beard down the chin — the same sign also means male and masculine.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a C, index finger and thumb slightly apart.
Hold the C hand upright before your torso, fingertips pointing forward.
Bring the hand straight down once, in a single smooth stroke.
Hold the C shape firm and the palm facing sideways during the drop.
Mouth the word 'person' silently, since the same sign also means student and pupil.
tip: One manual sign, three English words — mouthing selects person, student or pupil.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat and open, palm facing downward.
Raise the flat hand to about chest height in front of you.
Bob the hand down once, as if patting the top of a child's head.
Keep the palm facing down and the fingers together through the bob.
Smile gently — the sign carries the warmth of the pat itself.
tip: One pat means a child; repeat the bob while moving sideways and it becomes 'children'.

steps: Close your dominant hand, extending only the index finger upward.
Touch the fingertip to your cheek, just below the cheekbone.
Brush the finger downward along the cheek twice, with two light strokes.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your face through both strokes.
Mouth the word 'woman' silently — the same sign also covers girl and lady.
tip: One finger brushing the cheek twice; mouthing picks woman, girl or lady.

steps: Close your dominant hand, leaving the index finger extended straight upward.
Hold the extended fingertip against the side of your chin, close to the jawline.
Brush the finger along your chin, moving from your dominant side across to the other side.
Keep the finger pointing upward and the palm angled toward your face through the brush.
Mouth the word 'son' clearly, since the sign shares its handshape with 'boy'.
tip: The sign for SON shares its hand movement with BOY — the lip pattern tells them apart.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand relaxed in front of you, palm facing sideways.
Shape your dominant hand with the index finger and thumb pinched together.
Slide the pinched fingers up the ring finger of your non-dominant hand.
Move slowly from the knuckle toward the fingertip, as if fitting a wedding ring.
Smile gently and mouth 'wife', since the same sign also covers husband and spouse.
tip: One sign covers wife, husband and spouse — mouthing picks the English word.

steps: Extend the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand, closing the rest into a fist.
Hold the hand at chest height in front of your body, fingers pointing upward.
Glide the hand sideways to one side, then back again, in a small smooth motion.
Repeat the sideways glide two or three times, as if indicating two people.
Keep your palm facing forward and your expression neutral and inclusive.
tip: Fingerspelling M then F (mother, father) is the older form; the two-finger version suits any parents.

steps: Pinch the fingertips and thumb of your dominant hand together into a bunched shape.
Bring the bunched hand up toward your mouth, fingertips pointing inward.
Touch the fingertips lightly to your lips, as if placing food into your mouth.
Repeat the touch once more with the same small, crisp motion.
Keep your palm facing sideways and look toward your hand as you sign.
tip: The bunched-hand-to-mouth motion is shared with 'eat' — context and mouthing decide.

steps: Curve the fingers and thumb of your dominant hand into a C, like holding a small cup.
Lift the C hand to chin height in front of your mouth.
Tilt your wrist back and forth repeatedly, as if sipping from a cup.
Keep the motion gentle and rhythmic, with two or three easy tilts.
Mouth 'coffee' to fix the drink, since cup shares this handshape.
tip: The C-hand sipping motion is shared with cup; mouthing names the one you mean.

steps: Curve the fingers and thumb of your dominant hand into a C shape.
Raise the C hand to mouth height, as if holding a cup in your hand.
Tilt the hand back slightly toward your lips, as if taking a sip.
Repeat the small tilt once or twice with an easy, even rhythm.
Mouth the word 'cup' clearly, since coffee shares this sipping motion.
tip: Cup and coffee use the same C-hand sipping motion; your mouth pattern names the one you mean.

steps: Extend the index and middle fingers of both hands, keeping each pair together.
Point both finger-pairs downward in front of your body at chest height.
Bounce both hands up and down together in small, quick movements.
Keep the bounce lively, repeating two or three playful beats.
Smile as you sign — dog is a cheerful, bouncy sign.
tip: Two bouncing finger-pairs are the dog's legs on the move — keep the bounce small and quick.

steps: Curl the fingers of both hands into claw shapes, thumbs held out.
Hold both clawed hands in front of your chest, palms angled downward.
Circle the hands forward in repeated round motions.
Keep the circles smooth and even, two or three full loops.
Keep your gaze forward — the looping claws suggest all kinds of creatures.
tip: The generic ANIMAL sign is a catch-all; name the specific animal after it for clarity.

steps: Close both hands into fists and stack one on top of the other.
Hold the stacked hands in front of your body at waist height.
Move the hands up and down together, as if holding a pair of reins.
Keep the movement small and steady, like gentle tugs on the reins.
Lean slightly forward with an alert expression, as if riding.
tip: You are holding invisible reins — the up-down tugs name the horse.

steps: Open your dominant hand fully, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Hold the open hand out in front of you at waist height.
Push the hand forward while twisting your wrist from side to side.
Keep the twists small and repeated, like a fish wriggling forward.
Point your fingertips forward so the hand glides like a swimming fish.
tip: The wriggling wrist is the fish's tail — mouth 'fish' when you mean it as food.

steps: Curl the fingers of both hands into claw shapes, thumbs tucked in.
Touch the fingertips of both clawed hands to your cheeks.
Drag both hands outward from your cheeks in one smooth pull.
End with the hands slightly apart at face width, palms angled outward.
Narrow your eyes slightly, as if picturing the whiskers you traced.
tip: You are pulling a cat's whiskers outward from the cheeks — two quick drags work too.

steps: Close your non-dominant hand into a fist and hold it steady.
Lay your flat dominant hand on top of the fist, palm facing down.
Stroke the dominant hand forward over the fist, as if petting an animal.
Repeat the stroke a second time with the same gentle motion.
Keep your face soft and warm — you are stroking a small animal.
tip: You are literally stroking a small animal — the mime is the sign.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a firm fist.
Place the fist against the side of your cheek.
Brush the fist downward and slightly forward along your cheek.
Make the stroke short and definite, once only.
Keep the fist closed through the stroke — an open hand changes the sign.
tip: One firm downward brush of the fist — night darkening over the face.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, closing the other fingers.
Touch the fingertip to one side of your lower lip.
Sweep the finger along the lower lip toward the opposite side.
Repeat the sweep once or twice with a light, easy motion.
Mouth 'red' as you sign — the lips are busy in this one.
tip: Some signers swipe downward on the lip instead of across; the lower lip is the constant.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm in front of you with the palm facing up.
Open your dominant hand flat, fingers held together.
Rest the flat dominant hand lightly on the upturned wrist.
Rub in small circles, keeping the wrist movement controlled and local.
Keep the circles tight on the wrist rather than up the forearm.
tip: Blue rubs circles on the wrist — green slides along the forearm instead.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm in front of your body, palm facing down.
Shape your dominant hand into a closed flat hand, fingers together.
Slide the dominant hand along the top of your forearm toward the elbow.
Flick the hand upward as you reach the elbow, in one smooth finish.
Keep the sliding contact light — you are brushing the arm, not pressing.
tip: Blue circles the wrist; green slides the forearm — the location names the colour.

steps: Form the BSL fingerspelled letter G with your dominant hand.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, starting with the fingers closed.
Move both hands apart sideways while opening the fingers outward.
Make the opening bright and expansive, like spreading a treasure.
Mouth 'gold' to separate it from yellow, which signs up at the head.
tip: G gives the initial, the opening hands give the glitter.

steps: Touch your middle fingertip to your thumb, forming a small circle.
Raise the hand to the side of your head at temple height.
Flick the middle finger outward against the thumb, repeatedly.
Keep the flicks quick and light, two or three in a steady rhythm.
Keep your palm facing forward as the finger flicks.
tip: The repeated flick beside the head is yellow — one flick reads differently.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into a claw shape, fingers spread.
Place the clawed hand against the inside of your non-dominant elbow.
Drag the clawed hand along the underside of your forearm toward the wrist.
Keep the drag smooth and continuous in one steady stroke.
Hold the non-dominant arm still and relaxed throughout.
tip: BSL SignBank documents regional variants of BROWN; the forearm-drag form is the most widely taught.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, keeping the other fingers folded away.
Raise the fingertip to your face, near the cheek or the side of the nose.
Brush the fingertip downward in one smooth stroke, ending below the cheek.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your own face through the brush.
Pair the sign with a neutral expression, mouthing 'pink' as you sign it.
tip: Cheek or nose both occur — colour signs vary by region in the UK, so match your local signers.

steps: Hold both hands open and flat in front of your torso, fingers together.
Touch the middle fingertips of both hands lightly against your chest.
Drag both hands slowly upward across your chest without lifting them away.
Keep your palms facing inward toward your body for the whole movement.
Mirror the feeling with your face — soft and open for good feelings, tense for bad ones.
tip: Emotions live on the face in BSL — the upward drag means little without the expression to match.

steps: Close both hands into fists, leaving both thumbs extended and loose.
Press the knuckles of both fists together in front of your heart.
Push both hands a short distance forward, away from your chest.
Keep the thumbs pointing upward and relaxed through the movement.
Smile gently and mouth 'kind' — the warm face carries the meaning.
tip: Think of two fists offering goodness forward from the heart.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist, extending only the thumb upward.
Raise the fist to your face, placing the thumb tip against your chin.
Drag the thumb tip once across your chin, from your non-dominant side.
Keep the thumb angled upward and your palm facing inward through the stroke.
Smile as you sign — a flat expression can read as 'tidy' or 'clean' instead.
tip: One stroke across the chin with the thumb — 'Nice' lives at the jawline.

steps: Form a 'V' with your dominant index and middle fingers, folding the rest away.
Raise the hand up beside your eye, keeping the fingertips pointing upward.
Push the V handshape straight forward, away from your face.
Turn your palm to face yourself, keeping the fingers vertical through the push.
Look along your hand as it moves, so your gaze follows the 'seeing' direction.
tip: The two fingers stand for your eyes — the push shows the gaze travelling out.

steps: Hold both hands as flat blades, fingers together and straight, thumbs tucked.
Rest the flat edge of your dominant hand across the top of the other hand.
Tap the bottom edge of the upper hand against the top edge of the lower hand.
Keep both palms facing sideways, fingertips pointing across your body.
Repeat the small tapping motion twice, keeping your expression businesslike.
tip: One flat hand stacked on the other — like layers of effort piling up.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, folding the others away.
Raise the fingertip to the side of your forehead, near the temple.
Tap the side of your head once or twice with the fingertip.
Keep your palm facing inward and the finger pointing at the head.
Hold a thoughtful expression — the sign needs the 'thinking' face to land.
tip: Tapping the head shows thoughts happening inside — one or two taps is enough.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat, palm up, fingertips pointing forward.
Close your dominant hand into a fist, leaving the thumb extended.
Swipe the extended thumb sharply downward across the open palm.
Keep the open hand steady as the base while the thumb does the work.
Use a decisive expression — the firm swipe marks the beginning of something.
tip: The thumb 'switches on' against the flat hand — one crisp downward swipe.

steps: Hold both hands open and flat in front of your body, fingers together.
Turn both palms to face upward, as if holding two invisible balls.
Circle both hands continuously, the left going one way and the right the other.
Keep the circles small and even, just above waist height.
Smile — play is joyful, and a stiff face reads as mechanical.
tip: Two hands circling in opposite directions — nothing else in the dictionary moves quite like it.

steps: Close both hands into tight fists, keeping the thumbs tucked inside.
Hold both fists in front of your chest at shoulder width.
Pump the fists up and down in quick alternation, like pumping arms while running.
Keep the fists vertical, moving about a hand's length with each pump.
Lean your body slightly forward — the lean sells the running motion.
tip: Your fists become the pumping arms of a runner — alternate fast and short.

steps: Pinch the tip of your dominant thumb and index finger together, leaving the other fingers extended.
Bring the pinched fingertips to the corner of your mouth, just beside your lips.
Push the hand forward away from your mouth in one smooth stroke, keeping the pinch closed.
Hold your palm angled roughly toward the person you are asking.
Mouth the word 'ask' as you push forward, with your eyebrows slightly raised.
tip: Think of catching the question at your lips and tossing it to the listener.

steps: Make an open pinched handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingertips held apart.
Start the hand a short distance in front of your chest, palm roughly facing sideways.
Pull the hand back toward your chest in one decisive motion while closing the pinch shut.
Keep the movement single and firm, like plucking one option out of the air.
Pair it with a decided expression and mouth 'choose' as your hand closes.
tip: One pull, one close — the sign grabs the option and brings it home to you.

steps: Extend the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand, folding the other fingers away.
Hold the two extended fingers in front of your body, palm facing sideways like scissors blades.
Open and close the two fingers repeatedly in a small, quick snipping motion.
Drift the hand slightly forward as you snip, tracing the line of the cut.
Pair the sign with a neutral expression and mouth 'cut' while you snip.
tip: The same sign also covers scissors — BSL CUT mimes the tool doing the job.

steps: Hold both hands open and flat in front of your chest, palms facing toward you.
Cross your hands at the wrists while keeping the palms facing inward.
Sweep both hands upward and outward in a wide arc, as if tracing the rising sun.
Finish with your hands apart at about shoulder height, palms still facing you.
Keep a neutral expression and mouth 'day' as the arc completes.
tip: The sunrise arc is the memory hook — crossed hands uncross like dawn breaking.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat in front of your chest, palm facing upward.
Point your dominant index finger down into the hollow where the base hand's thumb meets the palm.
Hold the position steady for a beat — YEAR is fingerspelled as the letter Y, not signed.
Mouth the word 'year' clearly while you hold the letter shape.
tip: A single-letter fingerspell standing in for a whole word is normal for BSL time units.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell J, then A, then N with the two-handed BSL alphabet, keeping the flow smooth.
Let your dominant hand work over the steady non-dominant base hand for each letter.
Mouth the word 'January' as you fingerspell so your reader catches the month.
tip: BSL has no lexical sign for months — every British signer fingerspells them, J-A-N included.

steps: Form a closed flat hand with both hands, fingers pressed together.
Rest your dominant hand directly on top of your non-dominant hand at chest height.
Slide the top hand backwards until it lands on your non-dominant forearm in one smooth motion.
Keep both palms facing down while the base hand stays steady throughout the slide.
Mouth the word 'before' clearly as the top hand arrives at your forearm.
tip: The top hand physically moves backward — the direction of the movement carries the meaning.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of you in an open flat shape, fingers together.
Turn both palms to face upward, holding the hands level with each other.
Bounce both hands up and down together in unison, repeating the motion steadily.
Keep your palms facing up the whole time, the two hands mirroring each other exactly.
Mouth 'today' distinctly while you bounce — the mouth pattern separates it from NOW.
tip: The manual form matches NOW; the mouthed word 'today' is what pins it to today.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady as the base hand in front of you.
Fingerspell D, then E, then C with the two-handed BSL alphabet in one smooth run.
Keep the letters tight and connected so the abbreviation reads clearly.
Mouth 'December' as you finish the final C.
tip: Short months get three letters: D-E-C covers December for every British signer.

steps: Close both hands into fists with only the index fingers extended straight.
Hold your non-dominant fist out in front of you with the forearm pointing outward.
Start your dominant fist at the elbow end of your non-dominant forearm.
Slide the dominant fist along the forearm until the two fists meet.
Keep both palms facing sideways and mouth 'week' as the fists touch.
tip: One slide marks out the length of a week along your arm — seven days, one sweep.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space at chest height.
Fingerspell J-U-N-E with the two-handed BSL alphabet, flowing from letter to letter.
Work your dominant hand over your non-dominant base hand without pausing.
Mouth 'June' clearly as the spelling completes.
tip: Short months are spelled in full — four quick letters, J-U-N-E, with no abbreviation.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady as your base hand.
Fingerspell O, then C, then T using the two-handed BSL alphabet.
Keep the three letters flowing in one continuous, unbroken motion.
Mouth 'October' as you land on the final T.
tip: O-C-T is the accepted BSL form — the month lives in the fingerspelling, not a sign.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell M, then A, then R with the two-handed BSL alphabet in a smooth flow.
Keep your non-dominant base hand steady while the dominant hand forms each letter.
Mouth 'March' distinctly as the spelling finishes.
tip: M-A-R is the standard BSL form — same abbreviation convention as every other month.

steps: Hold both hands up in the fingerspelling space at chest height.
Fingerspell S, then E, then P with the two-handed BSL alphabet, flowing smoothly.
Keep the letters connected so the abbreviation reads as one unit.
Mouth 'September' as you finish the P.
tip: S-E-P is standard, though some signers add the T — Sept and Sep are both understood.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell J-U-L-Y with the two-handed BSL alphabet in one fluid run.
Let your dominant hand shape each letter over the steady base hand.
Mouth 'July' clearly as the final Y completes.
tip: Short months are spelled in full — J-U-L-Y, the whole word, with no shortcuts.

steps: Raise your dominant hand and form a V shape with your index and middle fingers.
Hold the V hand in front of your body at chest height, palm facing sideways.
Twist your wrist so the fingertips rock back and forth in small repeated swings.
Keep the movement tight and rhythmic, repeating it two or three times.
Pair it with a neutral expression and mouth 'again' as the V rocks.
tip: The rocking V replays the same motion — repetition is built into the sign itself.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady in front of you as the base hand.
Fingerspell A-P-R-I-L with the two-handed BSL alphabet, keeping the letters flowing.
Move your dominant hand smoothly from one letter to the next without stopping.
Mouth 'April' as you complete the final L.
tip: Longer month names are spelled out in full — A-P-R-I-L rides the fingerspelling alphabet.

steps: Hold both hands in a closed flat shape, fingers pressed firmly together.
Raise them in front of your chest with both palms facing toward you.
Sweep your dominant hand up slightly, then brush it swiftly downward across your non-dominant palm.
Make the downward brush quick and decisive, ending just below the base hand.
Shake your head firmly once as the hand brushes down, mouthing 'never'.
tip: The sharp downward brush 'wipes out' the idea — a definite no to every time.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell A, then U, then G with the two-handed BSL alphabet in a smooth flow.
Keep your base hand still while the dominant hand shapes each letter.
Mouth 'August' distinctly as the G lands.
tip: A-U-G is the standard abbreviation — three letters, fingerspelled, no lexical sign needed.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady as the base hand at chest height.
Fingerspell F, then E, then B with the two-handed BSL alphabet.
Keep the letters tight and flowing in one continuous movement.
Mouth 'February' as you finish the B.
tip: F-E-B follows the same three-letter abbreviation pattern as January's J-A-N.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat in front of you, palm facing upward.
Make a clenched fist with your dominant hand, thumb extended outward.
Rest the dominant fist directly on top of the open base palm.
Brush the fist back and forth across the palm repeatedly, knuckles grazing it.
Keep the brushing steady and unbroken, mouthing 'always' throughout.
tip: The never-stopping brush is the point — ALWAYS means the action does not end.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm stiffly in front of you with a closed flat hand.
Raise your dominant hand in a closed flat shape, held vertically above the other.
Bring the dominant hand down and land it firmly on your non-dominant forearm.
Keep the landing single and decided, palm facing down on contact.
Mouth 'early' as the hand lands, with a matter-of-fact expression.
tip: The hand lands high and early on the arm — the sign arrives before the wrist does.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady in front of you at chest height.
Form the fingerspelled letter F with your dominant hand above the base hand.
Move the dominant fingers in a small circular motion over the stationary base hand.
Keep the circles tight and repeated, palm facing down toward the base hand.
Mouth 'Friday' clearly while you circle the F.
tip: Some signers tap the F twice instead of circling — both forms mean Friday.

steps: Make a closed fist with your dominant hand, index finger pointing straight up.
Hold the hand in front of your body at chest height.
Move the hand across your body while tilting your wrist from side to side.
Keep the index finger pointing upward through the whole sideways journey.
Mouth 'later' as you move, with a relaxed, unhurried expression.
tip: The finger waggles its way across your body — pushed into the future, not now.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and steady as your base hand.
Form the fingerspelled letter M with your dominant hand above it.
Tap the M down onto the base palm twice in quick succession.
Keep the base hand still, palm facing up, while the M bounces off it.
Mouth 'Monday' clearly on the double tap.
tip: One M, two taps — Monday is the only weekday that double-taps a single letter.
